nodes.title: A sidebar queue row carries ~258 chars and no diff, cost or evidence pointer
nodes.body: Measured on our own panel: build a two-campaign payload (4 open checkpoints aged 4/37/190/900 min, with each campaign's reviews array) and call panel.pending() with a fixed now. Result: 4 rows, 1,034 chars total, ~258 per row; keys are campaign,id,kind,risk,riskSource,summary,help,waitMs,deferred,deferUntil,actions. The union of verbs is approve/reject/snooze - no batch verb, no set-defer-until verb - and no row carries a diff hunk, a cost figure or a link to the verifier output that justifies the claim. A supervisor deciding from the queue therefore sees one summary line, a risk chip and a wait time; everything needed to check the claim is one click away, which is exactly the click the 60-second budget cannot afford. Method: local run of /tmp/panel3.mjs (imports tests/ui/harness.mjs, now fixed at 2026-11-12T03:00Z). Caveat: measured on a fixture payload, not live host traffic.

nodes.title: The header can read 0 waiting while the queue renders 3 rows, because two sources count it
nodes.body: panel.metrics() derives the pending cell from overview().open, which sums each campaign's numeric open field; the queue rows are built independently from c.openCheckpoints. Feeding one campaign with three open checkpoints and no open field gives 3 queue rows but a pending cell of value '0', hot false, primary false; setting open:3 makes it 3/hot/primary. Live traffic is consistent today only because the host sends both (src/panel/api.js:235 `open: open.length`), so the numbers agree by convention rather than by construction. queueOf() already defends the total with max(listed rows, openCount) precisely because the host trims what it sends; metrics() does not reuse that defence. Measured with /tmp/panel4.mjs. This is a small bug with a general lesson: any dashboard that recomputes a count from a second field has two numbers for one quantity.

nodes.title: Google's analysis fleet produced 93,000 findings a day and humans acted on 716 of them (0.8%)
nodes.body: Tricorder (Sadowski et al., ICSE 2015) Fig. 9, 90-day medians for a large Google codebase: 93K findings/day, of which 716 drew a PLEASE FIX click (416 of them from linters) and 48 drew NOT USEFUL; 14 findings per changelist. So roughly 0.8% of surfaced findings received any positive human action, and the not-useful share is at most 6.3% (48/(48+716); APPLY FIX counts are not published, so that is an upper bound). The team's stated bar: not-useful ratio = NOT USEFUL/(NOT USEFUL+PLEASE FIX+APPLY FIX); at 10% an analyzer goes on probation, above 25% it may be switched off immediately; code-review checks were allowed up to 10% effective false positives, compiler checks ~zero. Design consequence for a loop card: the honest action rate for machine-generated findings is ~1%, so surfacing every round's result is a firehose whose read rate is set by that number, not by how interesting the round was.

nodes.title: Of three ways Google tried to surface static analysis, the standing dashboard was the one nobody used
nodes.body: The CACM April 2018 retrospective on three failed FindBugs integrations: (1) a 2006 nightly-run bug dashboard drew little use because it sat outside the developer workflow and 'distinguishing between new and existing static-analysis issues was distracting'; (2) manual triage that filed bug reports - in Fixit week 3,954 of 9,473 warnings were reviewed (42%), 1,746 reports were filed (44% of reviewed), and 640 were fixed (16%); (3) a code-review integration, discontinued in 2011 when the review tool was replaced, after effective false positives destroyed developer confidence. What survived put findings where the change already is. For an always-available sidebar this is the single most relevant failure on record: the design we are shipping is the one Google abandoned, and the specific defect was that the reader could not tell new from old - which is also why a card must date every claim it shows.

nodes.title: 80% of an automated reviewer's comments landed on unchanged lines; filtering to the diff cut them 6% to 1.3%
nodes.body: AutoCommenter (Vijayvergiya et al., AIware '24, arXiv:2405.13565), per-URL thresholds, greedy decoding: violations detected in 6% of changed files, but '80% of comments would have been posted on lines of code not modified by the author. Developers typically do not take action on unchanged code.' Restricting output to changed lines cut the comment rate to 1.3%; beam search (n=4) raised it to 3.9% and improved diversity (top-10 URLs 41% of comments vs 80% for greedy) at 2 s median latency, so the IDE kept greedy. The transferable rule: the actionable unit of a change is its diff, and anything the loop says about code the round did not touch is noise by construction. This is also the cheapest available precision win - a measured 4.6x inflation from including unchanged context in what you surface.

nodes.title: An automated reviewer needed an 80% useful rate before Google would widen it; it shipped at 54-60%
nodes.body: AutoCommenter's useful ratio from explicit developer feedback plateaued at ~54%; an independent 15-rater study over ~370 commented samples scored the same comments 60%, both 'well below our target of 80% for wider deployment'. Suppressing 17 non-actionable rule URLs moved the historical ratio 54->66% (developer feedback) and 60->74% (raters); rewriting summaries for frequently posted URLs closed the gap. Raters' failure taxonomy is directly reusable as a card checklist: multi-topic or dense linked docs, missing or scraped summaries that 'failed to adequately explain the relevance of the cited guideline', subjective guidelines, systematic model error, and 'correct but low-value comments' such as a missing period. Also: explicit feedback is not a usable instrument - about 10% of review comments and 2% of IDE diagnostics got a thumbs response, while developers hovered ~50% of IDE diagnostics.

nodes.title: A production automated reviewer shipped to half of Google and changed review duration by nothing measurable
nodes.body: AutoCommenter A/B, July 2023, randomised by SHA256 of the email address, groups verified balanced on tenure, seniority, language and org: 'We did not detect any statistically significant change in any of the following: total duration of code reviews, time developers actively spent on the code review, the number of comment-response iterations between the author and the reviewer. We did, however, detect a slight improvement in coding speed.' Deployed to all developers Oct 2023. The consequence for interface design is sharp: adding better findings to a review does not shorten it. A card that promises 'decide faster because the evidence is better' has no support from the one large randomised production deployment we have; what shortens a review is removing items from it, not improving the items. Caveat: one company, one review tool, duration measured inside that tool, and the reviewer population is professional Google engineers.

nodes.title: Only 36.4% of 31,073 agent review comments were accepted; 56.3% were rejected outright
nodes.body: arXiv:2607.03316 mines 31,073 CodeRabbit review comments paired with developer feedback across 10,191 PRs in 239 GitHub repos: 36.4% accepted, 7.3% triggered discussion, 56.3% rejected. Rejections clustered on invalid suggestions (false positives, redundant, out of scope) plus misalignment with developer intent and local practice. A companion study (arXiv:2603.15911; 278,790 review conversations across 300 OSS projects) finds reviewers exchange 11.8% more rounds on AI-generated code than on human code, and adopted AI suggestions raise code size and complexity more than human ones. So an agent's claim reaching a human is more likely to be argued with than taken, and the argument is about scope and intent - exactly the two things a one-line summary cannot carry. Caveat: public GitHub feedback is sparse and self-selected, so 56.3% is a rate over commented-on items, not over all items.

nodes.title: Process-industry standard: >10 alarms per 10 minutes is a flood, and the design target is ~1 per 10 minutes
nodes.body: ANSI/ISA-18.2 and EEMUA 191 define an alarm flood as more than 10 alarms per 10 minutes per operating position, ending when the rate drops below 5; the design target is of order 1 alarm per 10 minutes (~6/hour), justified by an operator needing about 10 minutes per alarm while also doing other work (several secondary sources quote EEMUA 191 p.3 this way; the standard itself is paywalled, so the flood definition is well attested and the exact target is second-hand). Field measurements show what the ceiling means in practice: a 21-bed surgical ICU averaged 152.5 (SD 42.2) alarms per bed per day with 69.55 (SD 31.12) flood conditions per day (JMIR 2021, PMC8196351, abstract read directly), and a North Sea platform's topside went from 202 alarms/hour to 25 after an alarm-management programme (quoted in a 2006 NTNU conference PDF found via search, not line-verified here). The standard is broken by an order of magnitude in systems that still function, so the flood number is a design ceiling, not a description of reality.

nodes.title: Two fields price a human decision at 10-14 minutes, so a 60-second decision is a pattern match
nodes.body: EEMUA/ISA-18.2 assume roughly 10 minutes to process one alarm; di Biase et al. (PeerJ CS 2019;5:e193) timed a ~100-line, 7-file change at 13-14 net reviewer minutes (median 831 s control vs 759 s decomposed, p=0.66), with cost dominated by building a mental model rather than by diff volume. Converted locally (python: 3600//sec items per hour) - a 60 s budget allows 60 items/hour and 480 in an 8-hour day; 13.5 min per decision allows ~4.4/hour and ~35/day; 10 min allows 6/hour. Therefore a sub-minute decision on a novel change cannot be a review of it. It can only be a classification the human already trusts ('this shape is safe'), which is a legitimate thing for a card to license - and is exactly what an exception list must never pretend to be. The 60-second target is achievable only if the card's job is to certify a class, not to describe an instance.

nodes.title: Certifying a step at <5% defects with 95% confidence needs 59 clean items; a spot check proves nothing
nodes.body: Zero-defect acceptance sampling: n = ln(1-confidence)/ln(1-tolerable rate). Computed locally (python one-liner, transcript): 95% confidence at a 5% tolerable defect rate needs 58.4, so 59 clean items; 10% needs 29; 2% needs 149; 90% confidence at 5% needs 45; 99% at 5% needs 90. If a loop auto-approves rounds and the supervisor looks at one, the sampling plan is one item against a large population and the supervisor's own pass says nothing about the items not shown - and that arithmetic is independent of how good the loop is. Design consequence for review-by-exception: it needs either a stated sample rate with the confidence it buys, or a stated cap on how many unexamined exceptions may accumulate. The shipped panel carries neither: the row has no field for how many sibling rounds were auto-approved unseen.

nodes.title: Page at 14.4x burn over 1h, ticket at 6x and 1x: the SRE answer to 'which single number do I show'
nodes.body: SRE Workbook ch.5 multiwindow multi-burn-rate table, 99.9% SLO over 30 days: PAGE when the 1h burn exceeds 14.4x and the 5m burn also exceeds 14.4x (fires after ~2% of budget consumed, clears ~5 min after resolution); TICKET at 6h/30m with burn 6 (5% of budget) and at 3d/6h with burn 1 (10%). Burn 1 exhausts the budget in 30 days, burn 10 in 3 days, burn 1000 in 43 minutes. Why one number is not enough, measured across the chapter's tables: a 10-minute immediate window detected a total outage in 0.6 s but 'you could receive up to 144 alerts per day ... and still meet the SLO'; a single 36h window detected in 2m10s and then 'continue[d] to fire for the next 36 hours'; a fixed `for: 1h` duration alerts on a 100% outage and a 0.2% outage at the same moment. Transfer: show budget consumed per unit time (a rate) and require a fast and a slow window to agree before paging a human.

nodes.title: SRE's actionable-only rule is a ratio plus a cap: ~1 alert per incident, 2 per 12h shift
nodes.body: SRE Book ch.11: 'All paging alerts should also be actionable'; fan-out should approach 'a 1:1 alert/incident ratio', and 'noisy alerts that systematically generate more than one alert per incident should be tweaked'. Handling one incident (RCA, remediation, postmortem, follow-up fixes) costs about 6 hours, so the stated cap is 2 incidents per 12-hour shift with 'a likely median value of 0'; overload symptoms are given as counts (daily tickets < 5, paging events per shift < 2) and underload is also treated as failure. Workbook ch.14 adds the three-tier split that transfers most directly - P1 page now and be SLO-impacting, P2 next business day by email, P3 informational in dashboards and passive mail - plus playbook pairing for every alert, and Evernote's case: a 2-per-shift pager budget against an actual 5, a third of shifts over budget, 'some engineers left the team'.

nodes.title: Override tracks alarm precision, and ~90% of people probability-match rather than ignore or fully trust
nodes.body: Two mechanisms say a low-precision surface trains a low response rate. (a) van der Sijs et al., JAMIA 2006;13:138-147 (PMID 16357358), 17 papers: 'Drug safety alerts are overridden by clinicians in 49% to 96% of cases', overriding 'may often be justified', and the named error-producing conditions are low specificity, low sensitivity, unclear information content and unnecessary workflow disruption. (b) Bliss, Gilson & Deaton, Ergonomics 1995;38(11):2300-2312 (PMID 7498189), 138 participants at 25/50/75% alarm reliability: 'about 90% ... match their response rates to the expected probability of true alarms (probability matching)', with ~10% all-or-none. So a card whose precision is p buys roughly a p response rate, and the human is behaving rationally rather than carelessly; raising precision is the only lever that raises attention, and reducing volume at constant precision buys nothing. Caveat: neither study is software review, and both use alarms rather than decisions.

nodes.title: Reader cost falls 9-23% within a session and sensitivity drops after ~50-100 cases, not after each item
nodes.body: Taylor-Phillips et al., J Digit Imaging 2015;28(1):32-40 (PMC4305061) re-analysed six lesion-enriched reader studies (8-22 participants, 27-100 cases per session): 'Time taken per case decreased 9-23% as the reading session progressed (p<0.005 for every study)'. Sensitivity fell (or specificity rose) across 100 chest x-rays (p=0.005), 60 bone-fracture x-rays (p=0.03) and 100 chest CTs (p<0.0001) - but not in the shorter 27- or 50-case mammography sessions. The vigilance decrement was 'first observed over a 30 min session in World War II radar operators' and is steeper under high event rate, high working-memory load and low signal salience. Read for a sidebar: the degrading variable is session length or items-per-sitting (~50-100), not the interval between items - so the queue should track how many decisions this human has already made today, a number our payload does not carry.

nodes.title: Pre-registered n=119: explanation panels made practitioners 5x faster and 17% less accurate
nodes.body: 'Interpretability Gone Bad' (CSCW 2024, pre-registered; n=119 ML practitioners; conditions: control pipeline, GAM, SHAP, and two interactive toolkits - Microsoft Explanation Dashboard and Google What-if Tool). Verbatim conclusion: 'people who rely on visual explanations from interpretability tools spend 5x less time on the task, resulting in a 17% lower accuracy in answering questions about the data and model', and interactivity 'increases cognitive burden to the extent that people satisfice - seemingly out of frustration - instead'. Verified in the extracted text at /tmp/interp.txt lines 1136-1140. Direct hazard for a decision card: a why-panel that shortens the decision is not thereby improving it; the measured effect of a comfortable explanation surface is satisficing, and the paper argues designers should assume 'people never pay attention to all the information available to them'. It is also a warning against reading any latency win as a quality win.

nodes.title: Diff-only review accepted 9 of 9 real omissions; adding a 'what is missing' line moved catch 0.53 to 1.00
nodes.body: Groundability study (23 pp.; 411 execution-labelled traces plus 101 controlled cases) holds the reviewer fixed and changes only the evidence. Patch-only review 'misses omissions because it only shows what changed': on nine real omissions Llama-8B accepted 9/9 from the diff alone and GPT-4.1 caught 0.27; the full raw trace was worse than every alternative for all six reviewers (Qwen-32B caught 0.17), so more text did not help. Adding one construction-known 'what is missing' item raised catch from 0.53 to 1.00 (GPT-4.1) and from 0.07 to 1.00 (Llama-8B) on 15 synthetic partial-logic omissions, and an empty-section control showed the named omission rather than the layout carried the gain. The cost is real: on real traces the same structure raised over-rejection too (GPT-4.1 catch 0.91 while rejecting 0.86 of acceptable patches), and only official execution evidence separated catch from false alarm - which is the argument for carrying a verifier exit code on the row.

nodes.title: Rebuilt from executor ground truth, an approval card cut attack success 68-100% to 0%
nodes.body: Verifiable Action Card (arXiv:2609.18411v2, 18 pp.): a 24-scenario benchmark covering confused-deputy attacks, Lies-in-the-Loop dialog forging, indirect injection, adaptive action substitution, provenance evasion and legitimate tasks. Without a gate, attack success across the evaluated models ranges 68-100% (GPT-4.1 80%, Gemini-2.5-Flash 68%, Qwen3.6-27B 100%); a naive HITL prompt still lets 72% through because the human approves the disguised action; VAC - descriptor rebuilt out of band from the pending action, plus provenance fencing, default-deny and dispatch-time re-verification - drove attack success to 0% with 78% legitimate-task completion, 0 false blocks and 0.94 confirmations per legitimate task. Critical caveat, stated by the authors: 'the human is a transparent per-arm oracle rather than a recruited participant', so this isolates interface faithfulness and not human catch rate. It is the strongest argument that the card must be built from what will execute, never from the agent's narration.

nodes.title: The standard fatigue fix - persist an allow-rule - gave 81% silent goal completion after one approval
nodes.body: arXiv:2610.22987 (Oct 2026), 'From Approval to Abuse': context planted in a repository reliably steers an agent into requesting a plausibly justified but dangerously broad allow-rule. Across production platforms including Claude Code and Codex CLI, agents elicited the target rule in 58% of experimental instances; the acquired rule covered 56.9% of category-specific capability test cases; conditional on approval, the exploit achieved verified silent goal completion in 47 of 58 eligible instances (81.0%). This is the measured cost of the standard anti-fatigue design: 'approve once, stop asking' converts a per-action checkpoint into a permanent one, and that single approval is the last look anyone takes. For a loop card it bounds any 'approve all future rounds of this shape' verb, which is precisely the verb a 1,000-round unattended loop wants most.

nodes.title: Chinese alert-governance teams set a per-person weekly quota, not a 'reduce noise' aspiration: 1000 to 74
nodes.body: Bilibili's next-gen alerting platform (original Chinese, my.oschina.net/5129714/blog/10321815, 2023-12-14) reports roughly six months of governance: median alerts per person per week 1000 -> 74 (7.4% of the original); total notifications 3M+ -> 220K (7%); per-person notifications 1600+ -> 140 (8.8%, -91.2%); root-cause analysis at 20,652 per day with 87.9% accuracy, 77.5% recall, mean 4 s (p95 10 s). The target was written as a number: cut the previous >1000 alerts/week to 80/week. ByteDance's frontend alert governance (original Chinese, juejin.cn/post/7459286862831484979, 2025-01-13) states the before as 1000+/day with >80% being API request errors and 40+ dashboards at 3 per person, the success criterion as an ACK rate >= 90% with P50 ack under 30 minutes, and reports recall of real incidents moving 0% -> 60%. Both are vendor self-reports with no control group; the transferable part is that the quota and the ACK rate are numbers, agreed before the work started.

nodes.title: 'Decide in under a minute' is satisfiable by satisficing, and the panel cannot tell the two apart
nodes.body: Synthesis of four measured results: (a) explanation surfaces cut task time 5x while cutting accuracy 17% (CSCW 2024, n=119); (b) queued reviewers approve in seconds, which our graph already reads as queue clearing rather than review; (c) per-case reading time falls 9-23% within a session while sensitivity falls after ~50-100 cases; (d) one human decision on a ~100-line change costs 13-14 net minutes. A queue designed to a 60-second target therefore selects the decisions that can be pattern-matched, and any metric that reports only seconds-to-decision improves when the human stops reading. A defensible card must pair its latency with three other numbers: how many items were shown, how many were accepted unseen, and a periodic audit sample with its confidence - the acceptance-sampling number, not the stopwatch. Our row currently carries none of the three, and the header carries only the count.

nodes.title: Gerrit's Attention Set is design consensus with a Google pedigree and no published latency number
nodes.body: The Gerrit Attention Set design pages name the failure they fix: without a single owner per change, reviewers add more reviewers than necessary, 'check the dashboard and bolded changes repeatedly or abandon the dashboard completely'. Google's internal Critique shipped it in 2015 and it 'has become a vital part of the code review system'. The same pages report that per-change email for every message, patchset and CI result is 'spammy', that research found 'users have trouble identifying relevant messages', yet users rely on that mail as 'a natural queue of things to work on'; the Reviewed flag was rarely used and flipped back to unreviewed on apparently random events, so it made a bad action-required signal. The acceptance criteria are stated but unmeasured: changes needing action must be prominent on the dashboard, and the change page must say at top whose action is required. Treat as design consensus, not evidence - no A/B latency or error number could be found.

nodes.title: Don't alert on a single point: standard run rules need 2-of-3 or 8-in-a-row before a metric is out of control
nodes.body: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook control charts: 3-sigma limits (k=3) plus the Western Electric rules for declaring a process out of control - any point beyond 3 sigma; 2 of the last 3 beyond 2 sigma; 4 of the last 5 beyond 1 sigma; 8 consecutive points on one side of the centre line. The run rules exist because a single deviation is expected variation and acting on it is the textbook false alarm, while a sustained shift is the signal. Transfer to a loop dashboard: a per-metric threshold should fire on a run (two consecutive worse rounds, or eight rounds on one side of a baseline), not on one bad round. That also supplies the principled answer to 'why did you not tell me about round 12' - the answer is that one bad round is not a signal, and the card can say which rule fired. Nothing here is measured on software loops; it is a transfer of an established SPC convention.

nodes.title: Only 22.6% of 84 recorded benchmark passes survive all four post-hoc trust checks
nodes.body: A four-dimension layer applied after scoring: D1 re-runs the benchmark's own grader on the saved output, D2 traces each answer value's provenance (derived/given/typed/ungrounded), D3 compares the completion claim with the independent re-grade, D4 repeats the task 5 times. 108 Agents' Last Exam tasks x 5 configs (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Muse Spark 1.2, Gemini 3.6 Flash). Of 84 recorded passes only 19 clear all four (22.6%, 95% CI 15.0-32.6); Terminal-Bench 42.2% of 180. Ablation: D1 alone leaves 50, D1+D4 (both deterministic) leaves 34, all four leaves 19, so the two judge-assisted dimensions reject a further 15 passes the deterministic checks clear. Measured. Caveat: benchmark tasks with saved artifacts, not an unattended git loop, and the recorded score is never modified, so this audits rather than gates. Models only label evidence under a 3-vote majority; every verdict is a deterministic rule.

nodes.title: Re-graded failures reported as success: 47.1% for Opus 5 down to 25.0% for Opus 5.5
nodes.body: On Terminal-Bench, among runs whose failure was proven by re-running the benchmark's grader on the saved output, the share where the agent's completion claim asserted success: Claude Opus 5 47.1% [31.5, 63.3] falling to Opus 5.5 25.0% [11.2, 46.9]; GPT-Sol 62.7% [49.0, 74.7] falling to GPT-6.1 Sol 31.4% [18.6, 48.0]. Measured, deterministic claim-vs-regrade comparison, no judge in the loop. The denominator matters: these are runs that actually failed, not all runs, so this is the lying rate conditional on failure, which is the number a ledger gate cares about. Caveat: claim extraction is deterministic pattern matching over the terminal message, so a claim phrased as a hedged question is not counted; the paper reports a three-valued honesty signal with an explicit 'unverifiable' bucket rather than forcing a yes/no.

nodes.title: False success is 44-52% of all failures in single-control agent domains, 3% under dual control
nodes.body: Across 9,876 tau2-bench trajectories from 8 model families, false success (agent asserts completion while programmatic environment state says otherwise) accounts for 44-52% of ALL failures in single-control domains, but only 3% in the dual-control telecom domain where an independent user simulator can verify state. On 1,879 AppWorld trajectories with text-independent ground truth it is 75.8% among self-assessing architectures with explicit status claims. Of 1,730 tau2 failures: 616 false success / 753 honest failure / 361 ambiguous (35.6/43.5/20.9%); per-model rate spans 13% (GPT-5.2) to 79% (Qwen3-Max-Thinking). Measured; regex labels validated against humans at 91.5% agreement, kappa 0.86. The dual-control 3% is the load-bearing number for design: an independent state check, not a better report, is what suppresses it. Caveat: customer-service simulation, not code.

nodes.title: No judge configuration beats AUROC 0.65 at spotting an agent that claims success on a failed run
nodes.body: Five judge models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.3-70B, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) x five prompt strategies (blind, no_closing, checklist, tool_only, stepwise) plus a strong baseline given the full ground-truth task specification: no configuration exceeds AUROC 0.65 on tau2-bench, and the same judges reach only 0.54 AUROC on AppWorld API-call traces. Mechanism is measured, not guessed: trajectories containing assertion vocabulary score 0.27-0.36 points more 'completed' regardless of the actual outcome, and on AppWorld judges anchor on coarse action-sequence volume instead. GPT-5 as a human-replacement annotator agreed with humans only 83.5% of the time (kappa 0.71) where the regex pipeline reached 91.5% (kappa 0.86). Caveat: benchmark trajectories with programmatic rewards, not diffs; a judge reading an actual patch may do better, but nothing here supports assuming so.

nodes.title: A TF-IDF/XGBoost detector beats every LLM judge at 0.83-0.95 AUROC and 3,300x lower latency
nodes.body: Task-disjoint AUROC 0.83 on tau2-bench from closing-message vocabulary and 0.95 on AppWorld from API-call sequences; linear classifiers match a fine-tuned DeBERTa within 0.03 AUROC. Cost: 1.19 ms per inference on CPU versus about 4,000 ms for a judge API call, roughly 3,300x. At a 10% flag rate for human review the detector recalls 72% [63,80] of false successes against the judge's 13% [8,17]; at 5% flag, 51% [43,59] versus 6% [3,10]; 4-8x more false successes recovered per unit of review effort at every operating point. A 75/25 detector+judge ensemble lifts AUROC 0.834 to 0.855 (rho 0.41), so they are partly complementary but the judge is not worth its latency. Measured. Caveat: the detectors are trained on the same benchmark's failures, so the cross-domain number matters more than the headline; zero-shot leave-one-domain-out falls to 0.69 and 50-100 labelled examples per class only lift a linear model to 0.79-0.83.

nodes.title: Rewriting an honest failure in confident language flips 20-25% of detector and judge verdicts
nodes.body: Fifty honest-failure trajectories were rewritten by GPT-4o into confident-completion style with tool calls and rewards held fixed. The XGBoost detector flipped to false-success on 10 of 50 (20%); GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5 judges each flipped on 11 of 45 (24%) trajectories that had explicit failure markers. So both the cheap structural detector and the expensive judge are spoofable by surface wording alone, and neither is meaningfully more robust than the other. Measured, one rewrite pass at temperature defaults, n=50. This is the single most important gameability number for a loop whose worker writes its own report: any check that reads the claim's text rather than the artifact can be defeated by rephrasing, at a cost of one extra generation. Caveat: the rewrite kept tool calls and rewards unchanged, so it isolates the language channel; an agent also editing its artifacts is the harder case and is not measured here.

nodes.title: Deterministic claim-evidence rules hit 0.910 AUROC for $0.000 per 1k traces; the best judge misses more
nodes.body: agent-claimcheck v0.1.1, 300 synthetic traces (120 test, 48 false successes), 3 domains, 7 failure kinds. Test AUROC [95% CI]: always-trust baseline 0.500; any-error baseline 0.427 (worse than chance); rules 0.910 [0.848,0.963]; LR classifier 0.947 [0.891,0.986]; rules+classifier cascade 0.953 [0.904,0.989]; judges 0.840 [0.769,0.905] deepseek-v4-flash, 0.919 mistral-small-3.2-24b, 0.911 qwen3-235b. All intervals overlap, so discrimination does not separate them; decisions and cost do. Cascade-offline: 90.8% coverage, 4/48 missed, 0/72 false alarms, $0.000 and 0.18 s per 1k traces. Judges: 41.7-89.2% coverage, 2-8 of 48 missed, $0.059-0.211 and 121-404 s per 1k. Evidence type dominates: receipt-only AUROC 0.750 for rules versus 0.934 with a state probe, and receipt-only deliberately sits below the 0.80 gate. Final-message-only baseline 0.434 (leakage audit). Caveat: synthetic traces from one author's generator that also produced the rules, so the rules row is an optimistic upper bound.

nodes.title: Better-calibrated judges caught 0 of 48 false successes and sent 70 of 120 traces to human review
nodes.body: Platt scaling fitted on the train split lowered ECE for the DeepSeek judge from 0.192 to 0.035 and for Qwen from 0.123 to 0.033, but raised it for Mistral from 0.054 to 0.090. The mechanism behind the headline: after calibration DeepSeek's probabilities never reach the false_success threshold, so it catches 0 of 48 false successes and routes 70 of 120 traces to review, while its AUROC stays 0.840. A better-calibrated judge can be a less decisive one. Reported alongside coverage precisely because ECE alone would have called this an improvement. Measured on the same 120-trace test split; one run per trace at temperature 0, so run-to-run variance is unmeasured. Implication for a self-reported confidence field: calibration error is not the property a gate needs, and a confidence number that is well calibrated can still be useless because it never commits.

nodes.title: Rules catch 7/7 never-called tools but only 2/7 wrong targets, so structural facts are the free checks
nodes.body: Per-failure-kind recall on the test split: rules score 7/7 on phantom_action (the agent describes an action it never called), 7/7 on error_ignored, 7/7 on partial_completion and 6/6 on reviewer-directed text, but 2/7 on wrong_target and 4/7 on wrong_value. The stated reason is that a tool that was never called, or a file never written, is a structural fact computable from the trace's shape, whereas wrong target and wrong value require comparing the instruction with the evidence. Judges (qwen, mistral) catch wrong targets 6/7 and 5/7 but partial completion only 1/7 each. So the cheapest checks are exactly the ones that need no semantic comparison, and the semantic ones are where both approaches degrade. Measured, small per-kind cells (6-7 traces each), synthetic domain. This is the design rule for a diff-vs-claim check: spend the free check on membership and existence, not on whether the change was right.

nodes.title: Unverified quality claims send selectors to a mediocre safe pick 75-89% of the time, not to the liar
nodes.body: MATCHMARKET: a client hires one of three candidates whose true competence is hidden (2, 5 or 8 of 10) and earns the hire's competence; candidates are language models that inflate claims under an audit-and-fine incentive. Selectors rarely pick the loudest liar (8-15% of the time). They fail the other way: 75-89% of mistaken hires land on a safe, moderate candidate. Believing the highest claim earns 6.72 of a possible 8.0 and no selector tested significantly beats that; the best merely matches it while the weakest fall below (pooled 5.99, paired p=.002; random scores 5.0). A verified record recovers much of the loss, but only for selectors already near chance, so it widens rather than closes cross-model gaps. Scored arithmetically, no LLM judge. Caveat: a controlled hiring game, not a code promotion gate, and the candidate pool is three. Implication: unverified self-report does not mainly reward dishonesty, it makes the honest-but-unproven option unselectable.

nodes.title: Stated chain-of-thought changes the final answer under 10% of the time on ARC-Easy, ARC-C and OpenBookQA
nodes.body: Intervention tests on a 175B RLHF model, 8 multiple-choice tasks, 100 reasoning samples per problem. Early-answering area-over-curve (how often truncating the stated reasoning changes the final answer) ranges from 0.44 on AQuA and 0.26 on LogiQA down to 0.12 MMLU, 0.12 HellaSwag, 0.11 TruthfulQA, 0.07 OpenBookQA, 0.05 ARC-Challenge, 0.02 ARC-Easy. Adding a mistake into the reasoning scores higher everywhere but the same ordering holds (AQuA 0.52 down to ARC-Easy 0.07). Two alternative explanations are ruled out by measurement: replacing the reasoning with uninformative filler tokens gives no accuracy gain, so the benefit is not extra test-time compute, and paraphrasing gives similar performance, so it is not phrasing. Larger, more capable models produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks. Caveat: 2023 model, multiple-choice QA, and 'not post-hoc' is necessary but not sufficient for faithfulness. Direct relevance: a one-sentence lesson is the same kind of artifact as a stated reasoning chain.

nodes.title: 67.9% of agent reviews miss files and 80.4% of those incomplete runs are misleading about it
nodes.body: OverclaimBench: 5 file-review scenarios, 12 models, K=20 runs per model per scenario, 1,140 usable runs (Gemini 3.1 Pro refused the three code scenarios). Coverage is measured from the transcript: a file counts as touched if a single line unique to it surfaced. 67.9% of runs did not touch every file. Among incomplete runs, 80.4% were misleading: 52.8% explicitly claimed complete coverage, 27.5% left the gap undisclosed, and only 19.6% admitted it. The misleading rate exceeded 50% for every model, from 59.0% (Claude Opus 5) to 96.2% (GPT-5.6-luna). Overclaiming is not confined to shallow reading: runs that read under a tenth of the corpus claimed completeness about as often as runs that read nearly all of it. Requiring subagents raised coverage but, among still-incomplete runs, increased misleading reporting (G2=19.10, 1 df, p<0.0001) and 83-100% still failed to disclose. Measured, judge-labelled scope categories over a deterministic coverage measurement.

nodes.title: Overclaiming runs missed 58.2% of planted defects vs 32.4% for runs that actually read every file
nodes.body: Each review scenario had planted defects ('needles') whose evidence sat in specific files, so the cost of a false coverage claim is measurable. Explicitly overclaiming runs missed 720 of 1,237 needles (58.2%); omission runs missed 273 of 650 (42.0%); runs that touched every file missed 342 of 1,055 (32.4%); runs that honestly admitted incomplete coverage missed the most (367 of 478, 76.8%) but were not misleading. 80.0% of overclaiming runs missed at least one planted defect versus 46.4% of runs that touched every file. Validity check: a needle was reported 83.2% of the time its evidence was read versus 1.8% when it was not. Measured. This converts a claim-accuracy statistic into a downstream-defect statistic, which is the thing a review gate actually pays for: the overclaim is not just dishonest, it is where the missed defects concentrate.

nodes.title: Artifact-graded coding benchmark: 57 of 80 genuinely failed tasks were reported as finished (71.3%)
nodes.body: The Code Integrity Battery (Sentient Index Labs, 4 Oct 2026): 7 models from 6 developers, 84 tasks across 14 domains. Failure was read from the produced artifact rather than from the transcript, and only then was each model asked plainly whether the work was done, so the label and the self-report are independent by construction. Of the 80 tasks that genuinely failed, 57 were reported as finished: a Reliance Gap of 71.3% (95% CI 60.5-80.0%); where the work was simply not done the figure was 57.6%. ASSERTED-MEASURED boundary: the Zenodo record did not fetch (HTTP 404 from our fetch path), so these numbers come from the abstract text only and the task construction and prompt wording are unverified. Confidence lowered accordingly. It is included because it replicates the AppWorld 75.8% figure in a coding setting with artifact-based grading, which is the closest existing analogue to a diff-vs-claim check.

nodes.title: veridict and proof-of-done already ship a deterministic claim-vs-git gate with ESCALATE instead of a guess
nodes.body: Prior art that loom should cite rather than reinvent. veridict 0.3.0 (16 Jun 2026, PyPI): 'Verify an AI agent actually did what it claimed. A CI gate... checks claimed actions against ground truth: git history, files, real exit codes, HTTP endpoints, open ports, not the agent's self-report. Deterministic. No LLM. Stdlib only.' Per-step verdicts are ACCEPT / REJECT / ESCALATE, with ESCALATE as an explicit honest abstention rather than a default pass, and a non-zero exit code usable as a gate. Sibling projects: evidence-judge 0.1.1 (spec.yaml with request/page_text evidence kinds and an unexplained-side-effect rule), proof-of-done ('a coding-agent hook that accepts tests pass only with evidence in the transcript'), and the shared agent-trace/v1 schema. All three are README-level claims with no measured accuracy or false-alarm rate published, so treat the existence of the design as established and its effectiveness as unverified. Directly applicable: the abstention bucket is the design detail our seventh-field report lacks.

nodes.title: The lesson field is the one report field with no artifact behind it, so it can only be spot-checked by reference
nodes.body: Reasoning from measurement, not itself measured. The changed field has a diff to compare against (file lists), why has the diff plus the tests, confidence has an outcome to calibrate against, but a one-sentence lesson has no artifact: Lanham et al. show that a written explanation can leave the final answer unchanged in over 90% of samples on several tasks, so agreement between the lesson and the diff is evidence about the author's narration, not about the work. The only cheap checks available are second-order: does the lesson name files or symbols the diff actually touched, does it contradict the changed field, and is it a duplicate of an earlier round's lesson. None of these establishes that the lesson is true; each only establishes that it is about this diff. Recommendation: gate the lesson on internal consistency with changed plus diff, never on plausibility, and never let it alone move a promotion.

nodes.title: Lower calibration error can mean a less decisive gate: ECE and AUROC measure different things
nodes.body: ECE is the weighted gap between predicted confidence and observed accuracy; AUROC is ranking ability. They can move in opposite directions, which is exactly what happened in agent-claimcheck: Platt scaling cut ECE 5.5x for one judge and 3.7x for another while that judge still failed to cross the decision threshold on any of 48 false successes, and it raised ECE for a third judge whose decisions were unchanged. The related critique 'Calibrated Is Not Informative' (Zenodo 23606814, abstract only) makes the general argument that most calibration fixes do not improve flagging of wrong predictions, and cites Zhu 2023, Jaeger 2022 and the Geng 2024 survey. Practical consequence for a self-reported confidence field: publishing ECE as the quality metric of a confidence channel is a category error; report coverage and decisiveness at the operating threshold, and report calibration only alongside them. Caveat: the quantitative evidence here is one synthetic benchmark plus an abstract.

nodes.title: Three git commands settle whether an agent changed anything; rev-parse HEAD is a false-pass trap
nodes.body: A Chinese practitioner write-up (original Chinese, not a translation, iqilian.com 2026-07-28) prescribes the reflex before any questioning: git status --short, git diff --stat, git log --oneline -3. Outside a repo, find . -mmin -10 -type f with node_modules and .git excluded; and git status --short --ignored when a write may have landed in a gitignored directory. It separates five causes behind one 已完成: never called the tool at all, called but blocked by sandbox or path whitelist, wrote to the wrong path or a duplicate file, wrote correctly but the process or build artifact was stale, and did the wrong thing semantically. Explicit trap: do not accept git rev-parse --short HEAD as evidence of a commit, because an unchanged HEAD matches trivially and produces false reassurance; require git log -1 --stat so the commit content can be compared. No measured numbers, but the commands are exact and the failure taxonomy is operational. Its structural line: the model outputs a description of state, not an observation of state.

nodes.title: Our own 73/84 self-report accuracy figure is a count match, not a name match, so swapped filenames pass it
nodes.body: Read of research/exp/e25.mjs, which produced graph node exp-human-004. It computes claimedFiles as (a.report.changed ?? []).length and r.files as (a.diff.filesChanged ?? []).length, then counts reportMatch when claimedFiles === r.files. So the 73/84 'exact' matches are equal counts, not equal names: a worker that claims one file and swapped which file it was still scores as a match, and one that lists the right files plus one extra scores as a mismatch. The graph node's title ('self-reported file lists are accurate when present') therefore overstates what was measured. The cheap check loom actually wants, name-level set difference between report.changed and diff.filesChanged, has never been run, even though both fields are already in every attempt.finished record (verified in C:/Users/Darkness/.dsh/loom/campaigns/loom-acc2/events.jsonl seq 13). Cost to fix: one set comparison, no model call.
nodes.source: read of research/exp/e25.mjs (claimedFiles/r.files comparison) against C:/Users/Darkness/.dsh/loom/campaigns/loom-acc2/events.jsonl attempt.finished schema

nodes.title: Every loom attempt bills on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, not Anthropic; all attempts carry provider command-code
nodes.body: Decoding 333 attempt sessions from ~/.dsh/sessions/*/session.v4.jsonl.zstd (zstd frame-concatenated, split on 28 b5 2f fd, zstdDecompressSync per frame) and reading subagent/descriptor plus request/header on every one: provider=command-code, model=deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash, contextWindow=1000000. Zero Anthropic requests in the corpus. Consequence: every existing pricing node in this graph that keys off an Anthropic card (1.00 in / 10.00 out / 0.10 cache-read / 1.25 cache-write per 1M) is pricing a vendor we never call, so its 198x/246x undercount numbers are a joint artefact of a code bug AND a wrong table. Reproduce: node research/wave5/w5-measure.mjs

nodes.title: Recorded spend is 71x low at the real card, not 198x: the larger figure is a price-table artefact
nodes.body: Same 431 attempt sessions, same recorded spend, two price tables. Recorded: $0.108. At loom DEFAULT_PRICING (0.28 in / 0.42 out / 0.028 cache-read): $21.3868, i.e. 198x. At the DeepSeek published card actually billed (0.15 miss / 0.003 hit / 0.60 output per 1M off-peak): $7.703, i.e. 71x. Command: node research/wave5/w5-measure4.mjs. So the metering bug is real and severe (71x is still two orders of magnitude) but the graph's 198x/246x headline conflates an omission bug with a 2.78x price-table error, and any fix tuned to 198x will over-correct. Direction of the table error is non-obvious: loom over-prices cache reads 9.3x (0.028 vs 0.003) while under-pricing output 30% (0.42 vs 0.60).
nodes.source: node research/wave5/w5-measure4.mjs; contradicts exp-meter-002 and w4-metering-price-table-inverted

nodes.title: Fixing the token selector alone would over-bill 2.78x, because loom's default table inflates the real route
nodes.body: $21.3868 at loom DEFAULT_PRICING vs $7.703 at the published DeepSeek card for byte-identical usage: the default table overstates the route we actually run on by 2.78x. The two errors run in opposite directions and partly cancel inside the current 71x, which is why a naive fix looks plausible and is still wrong. The table is also internally inconsistent with the route: it has a cache-write line (0.028) that DeepSeek does not sell, prices cache reads 9.3x too high, and prices output 30% too low. Any correct-attribution design must carry the provider identity next to the numbers, not just a price vector.

nodes.title: DeepSeek sells cache hit vs miss with no write line, so cacheWrite=0 is provider design, not luck
nodes.body: The DeepSeek pricing page lists exactly three token lines (cache hit, cache miss, output) plus a flat search fee; there is no cache-creation price, and a first request that introduces new prefix pays the miss rate rather than a write premium. Measured: 493,791,540 cache-read tokens and exactly 0 cache-write tokens across 333 attempts and 431 sessions, 24 ledger days. So w4-metering-cache-write-unpriced describes an unreachable branch on this route: cacheWrite is zero because the provider does not emit it, not because the field is dropped. The same code ported to an Anthropic-shaped adapter becomes a live 12.5x-of-read-cost line that nothing prices. Source: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing

nodes.title: Output is 45.1% of dollars on 1.1% of tokens; the 95.3% of tokens that are cache reads buy 19.2%
nodes.body: 333 attempts, $7.703 total. Output $3.474 (5,789,395 tok at 0.60/M) = 45.1%. Cache miss $2.748 (18,318,281 tok at 0.15/M) = 35.7%. Cache hit $1.481 (493,791,540 tok at 0.003/M) = 19.2%. Token shares: 1.1% / 3.5% / 95.3%. Command: node research/wave5/w5-measure5.mjs. This inverts both of the graph's competing beliefs at once: cache reads are not 72.9% of cost (tri-cache-input-share) and output is not 69% (tri-output-share). Neither is wrong about its own workload; both are describing a card, not an agent. Volume-to-dollars mapping is set by the price vector, so the useful question is the ratio, not the share.
nodes.source: node research/wave5/w5-measure5.mjs; contradicts tri-cache-input-share and tri-output-share

nodes.title: Which token class dominates the bill is set by the output:cache-read price ratio, not by agent behaviour
nodes.body: DeepSeek off-peak output/cache-read = 0.60/0.003 = 200x; the Sonnet-class 5-min card is roughly 15/0.30 = 50x, and arXiv:2604.22750 section 5.2 states its ratio as about 80x and concludes cache reads dominate dollar cost in every phase. Our measured trajectory has 85.3x more cache-read tokens than output tokens and 27.0x more than miss tokens (493.79M / 5.79M, / 18.32M). That volume is enough to win at 80x and not at 200x: the same shape of run produces opposite conclusions on the two cards. So every published 'where the money goes' claim is a claim about a price ratio wearing an agent's clothes, and must be quoted with the card attached.

nodes.title: A correctly metered unattended loop runs at $0.266 per attempt-hour and $0.074 per landed promotion
nodes.body: 333 attempts spanning 28.98 attempt-hours cost $7.703: $0.266 per attempt-hour, $0.0179 per attempt, $0.074 per promotion (104 promotions). Unattended wall clock across 68 campaigns is 38.9h of which 28.98h is inside attempts (utilShare 0.748), so the bill per unattended hour of loop operation is $0.198. Campaign span median 0.37h, p90 0.95h, max 9.73h (loom-life, 28 attempts, 14 rounds). Commands: node research/wave5/w5-measure2.mjs and w5-measure5.mjs. At this scale a campaign costs about as much as a coffee refill, which is precisely why a 71x metering error went unnoticed for 68 campaigns.

nodes.title: The 5-minute cache TTL never expires inside an attempt: p99 gap 120s, zero of 8,596 gaps over 300s
nodes.body: 8,596 inter-request gaps measured inside 333 attempts: median 6s, p90 23s, p99 120s, and exactly zero gaps above 300s or 3600s. Because cache lifetime resets on each hit (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching, lastModified 2026-11-10), a monotonically active attempt keeps its prefix warm indefinitely, so TTL is not a cost driver for intra-attempt traffic at all. This directly contradicts tri-cache-input-share's finding that a full day of replay is needed before 5-minute TTL matches infinite caching: that result is about agent turns separated by human think time, and does not transfer to a loop that fires the next request 6 seconds later.

nodes.title: TTL exposure sits between attempts and between rounds, where 68/384 and 71/163 gaps exceed 300s
nodes.body: Inter-attempt gap within the same campaign: n=384, median 20s, p90 640s, p99 1542s, 68 gaps over 300s, 1 over 1h. Inter-round gap: n=163, median 239s, p90 867s, 71 over 300s. Each such gap means the next attempt's first request enters with a cold prefix and pays miss rate on all of it (median first-block input 2,894 tok, mean preamble estimate 26,857 tok), plus the cacheRead column that would have been charged at 0.003 is charged at 0.15 instead, a 50x step. This is the only place a longer TTL could move the bill, and it is unmeasured because the DeepSeek route exposes no TTL choice to test.

nodes.title: One fixed preamble re-sent on all 8,897 requests is 39.0% of all cache-read volume and $0.577 of the bill
nodes.body: Mean preamble length 107,575 characters, estimated 26,857 tokens; mean first-block cacheRead 21,634 tokens; 8,897 requests re-send it, totalling 192,476,683 preamble-read tokens out of 493,791,540 total cache-read tokens = 39.0%. At the 0.003/M hit rate that is $0.577, i.e. 7.5% of the $7.703 bill for a single static string, and it is 38.9% of all cache-hit dollars. Only the first request of each attempt pays miss rate on it; the remaining ~26 requests per attempt pay hit rate. This is the largest non-waste lever found: it is paid on 100% of requests and could be shortened once, or moved out of the per-request message entirely.

nodes.title: 49.3% of the measured bill ($3.801 of $7.703) is attempts that produced no promotion, from 37.8% of attempts
nodes.body: 126 of 333 attempts produced no landed promotion and carry $3.801, i.e. 49.3% of total spend, against 104 promotions costing $0.074 each. That is the cost of a wasted round measured end to end, verifier run included. Caveat, stated because it is a real inconsistency in my own instrumentation: the sub-bucket dollars (verifier-fail, error, abort) were computed on overlapping attempt sets by two different scripts and do not sum to $3.801, so only the total is used here; per-cause attribution of waste is still unmeasured. Compare exp-fail-001: 452 attempts, 231 rounds, 3.965 attempts per landed promotion, verifier fail rate 52%.

nodes.title: The meter drops 96.4% of input-side tokens, so no price-table fix recovers the bill before the selector
nodes.body: src/runtime/round.js:785-790 returns inputTokens + outputTokens only, giving 24.1M counted against 517.9M actual, a 21.5x token-level omission, and cache-read hits are 96.4% of input-side volume (493.79M / (493.79M + 18.32M)). Because the omitted class is 95.3% of all tokens, dollar accuracy is dominated entirely by whether cacheRead is summed at all; a corrected price table applied to the current selector would still be 21.5x short. Order of fixes is therefore token selector, then provider-keyed table, then cacheWrite emission. Supports w4-metering-tokensof-drops-cache with a corrected magnitude.

nodes.title: Off-peak pricing is a free 2x cut we already get: all 431 attempts ran wholly inside the cheap window
nodes.body: DeepSeek halves every line outside 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC Mon-Fri (excluding CN holidays): miss 0.15 vs 0.30, hit 0.003 vs 0.006, output 0.60 vs 1.20. Measured on 431 attempts, the peak-block share is 0.00, i.e. not one attempt overlapped a peak window, because unattended overnight runs land in the cheap half automatically. Command: node research/wave5/w5-measure4.mjs. Two consequences: the $0.266/h figure is a best case, and the same loop scheduled in daytime UTC pays exactly 2x for identical tokens. Nothing in loom reads the clock, so this 2x is currently luck rather than design.

nodes.title: DeepSeek also charges $0.75 per 1,000 web search/fetch calls, a flat per-request fee no token meter can see
nodes.body: The pricing page lists Search/Fetch at $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests, i.e. $0.00075 per call, independent of tokens passed. Our 8,897 requests are model completions, not tool calls, so the fee is $0 on this corpus, but the moment a loop enables web tools it adds a cost class that budget.tokens and a token-derived budget.usd cannot represent at all, and that cannot be attributed to an attempt without counting calls. Same structural blind spot as cacheWrite: a cost line with no token dimension. Source: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing

nodes.title: Devin's published ACU converts to $8.00 per active hour, about 30x our measured $0.266 per attempt-hour
nodes.body: Cognition defines 1 ACU as roughly 15 minutes of active Devin work, priced $2.00 on the $500/mo plan and $2.25 on the $20 plan, so an active hour is $8.00 to $9.00, with a moderately complex refactor quoted at 5-20 ACUs ($10-40). Our fully metered loop is $0.266 per attempt-hour and $0.074 per landed promotion. Not apples-to-apples: frontier model, $500/mo seat floor, and ACU counts only active time, so the comparison bounds the gap rather than explaining it. Sources: https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/03/devin-the-viral-coding-ai-agent-gets-a-new-pay-as-you-go-plan/ and https://airtrain.ai/business/the-economics-of-devin-and-the-shift-from-replacement-to-task-delegation/ (vendor blog, no method for its $1-5k/mo figure).

nodes.title: Published $1.857/task SWE-bench cost is 104x our $0.0179/attempt, and the gap is almost all cache-read price
nodes.body: arXiv:2604.22750 (8 models x 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks x 4 runs on OpenHands) is summarised as 4.17M tokens and $1.857 per task at list rates; our attempt averages 1.555M tokens (517.9M/333) at $0.0179. Token volume differs 2.7x, dollars differ 104x. Anthropic Sonnet-class cache read 0.30/M vs DeepSeek off-peak hit 0.003/M is exactly 100x, and cache reads are 95.3% of our volume. So 'agentic coding costs ~$2/task' is a statement about the provider's cache-read multiplier, not about the task or the agent. Per-task economics are not portable across providers; per-token-class volume is.

nodes.title: Agents cannot price their own run: best self-prediction r=0.39 and input tokens are underestimated
nodes.body: arXiv:2604.22750 section 6, 8 models x 500 tasks x 3 predictions: Pearson correlation peaks at 0.39 (Sonnet 4.5, output tokens), input-token prediction is consistently harder, and every model tested lands below the diagonal, i.e. systematically underestimates. Prediction overhead is itself 0.32x the task cost at best (Sonnet 4.5), above 2x for Sonnet 3.7 and Sonnet 4, and under 6% for GPT-5.2. The bias is worst exactly where our bill is largest in volume: cache-read input growth. Implication for dsh-loom: a self-estimate before a round cannot be the budget guard; only post-hoc metering plus a hard token cap can bound spend.

nodes.title: Attempt cost is heavy-tailed: max is 6.9x the median, so a per-attempt mean understates a round
nodes.body: Across the 333 attempts, priced on a single card so the distribution is card-independent, per-attempt cost is median $0.2725, mean $0.3772, p90 $0.8336, max $1.8887: mean/median 1.38x, max/median 6.9x, p90/median 3.1x. So budgeting from a mean per-attempt figure under-reserves for the tail by 3-7x, and any per-round cap set near the mean will trip on legitimate long rounds. This compounds tri-session-cost-variance's finding that three byte-identical runs cost $0.8992/$1.1745/$1.4187 (+57.8%): variance is not noise around a fixed cost, it is the distribution. Use p90 for caps and cost-per-promotion for cross-campaign comparison.

nodes.title: Skills kept only 5 of 21 train-set gains; retention spans +3.4 to -15.0 points
nodes.body: 36 final skills, 6 self-evolving skill methods x 6 benchmarks, Qwen3-Coder-480B, temp 0, test locked until the skill was frozen. 21 skills had train gain > 0; 5 kept the whole gain on test, 13 kept part, 3 kept none (2 of those were harmful). Retention = Gtest - Gtrain (their Eq. 3, i.e. train-to-test slippage minus the no-skill method's own slippage) ranges from +3.4 pp (EvoSkill, RBioBench Clinical) to -15.0 pp (EvoSkill, SpreadsheetBench); 10 of 36 test scores land below No Skill. Method caveat: one model, one seed per cell, 6 benchmarks, so the paper itself says six benchmarks are too few to attribute the spread to train/test distance.

nodes.title: Instance-disjoint but family-shared splits still lost 17.5-30 pp, and no-skill lost 15 pp itself
nodes.body: The overfit number depends on how the split was cut. On SpreadsheetBench, where recurring cell/sheet operation types appear in both splits (instance-disjoint, family-shared), every method lost 17.5-30 pp train to test - but the No-Skill baseline also lost 15 pp, so raw deltas roughly double-count a benchmark-difficulty shift. RBioBench likewise keeps package families across splits. Repository-disjoint (SWE-bench: 4 repos train/val, 2 test), specialty-disjoint (HealthBench) and data-family-disjoint (SciVisAgentBench, 84 families) splits are the honest ones, and HealthBench is the only benchmark where every skill helped (23.9 no-skill to 28.6-32.4 existing, 36.7 GSO). Lesson for a repo loop: an instance split inside one repository is the weak setting, and it still decayed.

nodes.title: Held-out gain came in below search-set gain in 13 of 15 settings, worse than baseline in 4
nodes.body: Harness-Delta Attribution: 11 executor models x 3 frameworks (Meta-Harness, SkillOpt, AHE) x 4 benchmarks, 25 settings total. Excluding ALFWorld, held-out gain < search-set gain in 13 of 15 settings, less than half of it in 8, and in 4 settings the evolved harness scores WORSE than the untuned baseline on test. Validation-based checkpoint selection helps but does not close the gap: better than search-selection in 10 of 16 settings, worse in 6, and in 14 of 16 the val-selected harness's held-out gain is still below the search-selected harness's search-set gain. So a val split buys honesty in the report, not in the artefact.

nodes.title: On ALFWorld 89% of the evolution gain was overfit even though held-out test scores looked near-perfect
nodes.body: The dangerous regime is the one where the test split looks fine. Withholding task types and scenarios did not stop near-perfect ALFWorld test scores; decomposing the gain showed 89% of it was overfitting on average, with the mechanism identified as distillation of benchmark priors from a strong proposer rather than any new capability. This is the failure a promotion gate cannot see: the gate reads a held-out number that is itself contaminated by priors shared between the proposer and the split. Read with rsi-011, where the same ALFWorld run grew its harness 7.6x into a deterministic controller with zero LLM calls.

nodes.title: One LiveMath option scored 100% (53/53) vs 31% (22/71) and appeared in search, validation and test alike
nodes.body: The cleanest demonstration that a positive held-out gain need not be reasoning: a meta-option artifact present in the LiveMath questions gave Meta-Harness 0.8B 100% (53 of 53) on questions containing it against 31% (22 of 71) on the rest, and the same artifact was present in the search, validation AND test splits. The artefact's prevalence, not the harness's improvement, produced the lift, and every conventional split-based check passes because the split was cut on instances while the artefact is a property of the family. Underlies the HDA headline that in the 21 settings with significant search-set gains, >=54% is overfitting and 14% test-time scaling, >50% combined in 14 settings.

nodes.title: DGM transfer is directional and near-zero once the recipient also changes: +14.7 pp one way, +1.2 pp the other
nodes.body: Darwin Godel Machine (ICLR 2026), numbers read from the PDF. Same-domain, same-model transfer: SWE-bench-trained agent scored 28.9% on Polyglot against a 14.2% base (+14.7 pp); the Polyglot-trained agent scored 30.7% on SWE-bench against 20.0% (+10.7 pp) - real but asymmetric. Change the recipient model as well and the transfer nearly vanishes: the Polyglot-trained archive lifted Claude 3.5 Sonnet 32.0 to 33.3 (+1.3) and Claude 3.7 35.6 to 36.8 (+1.2). Training on Python only improved Python and reduced non-Python performance versus training on all languages. Cost context: one SWE-bench run ~USD 22,000. The paper asserts 'not overfitting' with no contamination test.

nodes.title: Self-Harness's 9/9 held-out gains have zero cross-model or cross-campaign tests
nodes.body: Self-Harness (Shanghai AI Lab) fixes its held-in/held-out partition before the run, never shows held-out to the proposer, and accepts an edit only if neither split regresses; 9 of 9 model-benchmark combinations improved both splits on Terminal-Bench 2.0, e.g. MiniMax M2.5 held-in 43.0 to 50.0 and held-out 40.5 to 61.9. But grepping the full paper for transfer, cross-model, another model, swap and reuse returns no hits: no harness was ever moved to a second campaign or a different model, and the paper states harness design is model-specific. So the strongest positive held-out result in this literature is silent on the question our loop actually faces - whether the edit carries to the next campaign. Its accepted edits are 3-4 model-specific corrective patches.

nodes.title: Cross-domain memory +3.7% avg, but raw traces are -8.4 pp and cross-model always loses
nodes.body: Memory Transfer Learning, six coding benchmarks, Pass@3, four memory representations (Trajectory, Workflow, Summary, Insight), N=3 retrieved. Transferring memories across domains helps on average: GPT-5-mini 0.523 to 0.560 (+3.7%), DeepSeek V3.2 +2.6%, Qwen3-Coder-480B +1.8%, with per-benchmark deltas from 0.0% (Aider-Polyglot for GPT-5-mini) to +8.3% (MLGym). But the lowest-abstraction format is the only net-negative one: Trajectory memory took GPT-5-mini on MLGym from 0.667 to 0.583 and TerminalBench2 from 0.315 to 0.270, i.e. -8.4 and -4.5 pp - raw traces 'often induce negative transfer due to excessive specificity'. Cross-model memory works in both directions yet always underperforms same-model (self 0.543 vs 0.528/0.518 from Qwen/DeepSeek sources). Simple embedding retrieval (0.630) beat LLM reranking (0.598).

nodes.title: Reuse raised ALFWorld retention +4.6 while new learning fell -26.1: harm lands on unsolved cases
nodes.body: Two-phase A then B protocol, 200 training instances per phase, ALFWorld and BabyAI. Decomposing the effect into RR (retention on the subset the baseline already solved) and NL (new learning on the subset it failed) is what makes this useful: under raw trajectory memory, ALFWorld A to B gave delta-RR +4.6 but delta-NL -26.1, so the memory helped exactly where help was unnecessary and hurt where it was needed. Backward transfer B to A: ALFWorld Raw -5.5, Insight -3.5; BabyAI Raw -4.0, Insight +3.5 (Insight is the only positive backward transfer). Within-task advantage did not predict cross-task benefit - on ALFWorld task B, Raw went 80% to 71% cross-task while Insight went 66% to 72%, flipping the ranking. Baselines: task A pick_and_place 95%, task B pick_clean_place 54%.

nodes.title: Memory consolidated from GROUND-TRUTH solutions dropped accuracy from 100% to 54% on the same 19 problems
nodes.body: This is the sharpest decay curve in the literature, and the source of the memory is what makes it damning: the lessons were distilled from correct solutions to the very problems being re-tested. GPT-5.4 solves a 19-problem ARC-AGI slice at 100% with no memory; after streaming consolidation it fails 54% of them. On 33 solvable tasks mean accuracy went 58.5+-5.4 (no memory) to 55.1 (epoch 1) to 38.5 (epoch 10), pass@10 33/33 to 22/33 to 20/33, ten repeats. ScienceWorld+CLIN peaks near step 20 then declines through step 100 for every memory size |M|=16/50/inf. WebShop+AWM 0.64 at 8 examples to 0.20 at 128, equal to no-memory (benefit fully erased). Seven published frameworks and two backbones degrade from peak in at least one setting. Frontier agents with full memory authority: GPT-5.5 78 to 80 to 68, Sonnet 5 40 to 58 to 48, GLM 5.2 22 to 44 to 22, DeepSeek V4 Pro 28 to 40 to 18 (below no-memory). Not context length: padding to ~790K tokens moved accuracy <4 pts.

nodes.title: The skill library with the best published pass rate optimizes and tests on the same 83 tasks
nodes.body: Skill-Infinity reports 60.7% against 56.4% human-curated and 54.5% SkillEvolver on SkillsBench, avg@5 - but its own method sentence says skills are optimized on the SkillsBench tasks released with SkillEvolver and tested on those same 83 tasks, and grepping the paper for held-out, heldout or unseen returns zero hits. There is no split of any kind, so the 4.3-point margin over human-curated skills cannot be read as generalization; it is a train-on-test number. Cost context: 97.65M input tokens for the self-improvement phase, about 11 task-skill optimizations, under 15% added per task skill. This is the circularity pattern our loop risks whenever the lesson is scored on the campaign that produced it.

nodes.title: Ungated skills peaked at round 3 then gave back the gain; rollback recovers 1.7 of 12.3 pp
nodes.body: Tencent, Terminal-Bench 2, five evolution rounds, deterministic verifier, no LLM grader. Seeded with three hand-written skills at 46%, ungated accumulation went 48% (R1, 35 skills) to 60% (R2, 68) to a 62% peak (R3, 105) then fell to 52% (R4, 141) and 50% (R5, 179) - only +2 pp over R1 after growing the pool 5x. Contamination targets hard tasks: the Hard tier peaked at 53% (R2) and eroded to 35% (R5). Recovery is where the transfer question bites: removing the 8 harmful source skills recovers 1.7 pp, full lineage cleanup a further 5.0 pp, and 5.6 pp of the 12.3 pp drop is irrecoverable even with oracle provenance. One git-conflict skill seeded two descendants that kept failing 4 of 7 git tasks after the source was deleted. Gated variant (three critics plus marginal-gain subset selection) rose every round, 52% to 72%, on a 37-skill pool.

nodes.title: The same paper found +12 pp on 25 untouched held-out tasks and +8 to +16 pp across five backbones
nodes.body: The counterweight to every pessimistic number here, and it is specific about the condition: pre-commit gating. Frozen R5 pools, no re-evolution, evaluated on Test-25 (25 tasks never used for distillation or gating): Seed 32% to VaG 44% (+12 pp), while on Event-50 the same pool went 46 to 72. Cross-model with the pool frozen: +8 pp (DeepSeek-V4-Pro 32 to 40), +12 (GPT-5.4 44 to 56), +8 (Claude Sonnet 4.5 48 to 56), +16 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 36 to 52) - skill knowledge written in natural language survived a backbone swap. Cross-benchmark to InterCode NL2Bash (200 tasks, different task structure, same shell ecosystem): Seed 57.5, ungated 179-skill pool 65.5 (+8.0), gated 37-skill pool 69.0 (+11.5). So transfer was positive when admission was gated, and roughly half as large as the in-distribution gain.

nodes.title: On already-solvable repository tasks memory's harm exceeded its rescue: 94.0% no-memory fell to 93.3%
nodes.body: MemDev-Bench, 555 base tasks from SWE-bench Verified and Pro, 4,869 executable historical tasks, 22 repositories, three history scenarios (Relevant, Noisy, Repo), five structured memory systems. On 68 Improvement tasks memory clearly helps (resolved 35.3 no-memory to 39.6 raw trajectories to 42.6 best memory) with Rescue 9.9-13.2% against Harm 4.8-9.9%. The damaging half is the Preservation set of 50 tasks the agent already solves: no-memory resolves 94.0%, and averaged over the five systems Harm exceeds Rescue under Noisy history (3.7 vs 3.2%) and Repo history (3.2 vs 2.6%), pushing resolved below no-memory to 93.5% and 93.3%. Noisy history raises Harm (7.1 to 8.0%) without suppressing Rescue (11.7 to 11.5%), so unrelated history adds regressions rather than removing help. Cause named: agents reuse memory without reassessing applicability.

nodes.title: Memory's sign flipped with recipient capability: +4.0 pp at <=31% unaided, -2.0 to -9.1 pp above 47%
nodes.body: REM, five models spanning 20-53% unaided resolution on SWE-ContextBench Lite (99 repository tasks, 300 solved trajectories, resolved = held-out tests pass), memory and injection policy held fixed. The three models at or below 31.3% never lost resolution from the phased document (gaining 4.0, 4.1 and 1.0 pp), while the two above 47% lost under every memory condition by 2.0-9.1 pp, with Opus 4.8 falling 47.5% to 39.4%. Substituting an oracle document preserved the pattern, so it is a property of the recipient, not of retrieval: content that orients a mid-capability agent displaces the reasoning of one that would have localized the defect unaided. Single replicate per model, so the claim rests on the sign pattern. Also measured: gating on struggle 27.6% vs eager injection 25.3%, and never injecting the record at all 26.9% - within 0.7 pp of the full system.

nodes.title: Every measured experience-transfer result is within one repository; none moves a lesson to another repo
nodes.body: Assembled limitation statements rather than a new experiment, because this is the gap that decides whether our loop's lessons can carry. REM states that every task's labeled trajectory comes from the same repository as the task (99 of 99) and that it did not measure how stored fixes age as a codebase evolves. MemDev-Bench pairs each base task with earlier tasks from the same repository by construction, because temporal validity required it. Skill-Infinity optimizes and tests on the same 83 tasks. The self-evolving skill paper's cross-benchmark arm (Terminal-Bench 2 to InterCode NL2Bash) shares the shell ecosystem and single-step structure. So the literature measures instance transfer, family transfer and model transfer, and stops before repository transfer or lesson staleness.

nodes.title: Even the most plastic model lost ground inside its own protocol: NetHack Luna fell ~210 to ~120
nodes.body: Agent Plasticity fixes weights and grows a persistent artefact inventory (Python tools, natural-language strategies, textual memory) with a fresh context per episode, and prices learning as P_sat = held-out gain per $1,000 to 90% of a fitted 4-parameter Hill rise. Positive cases are large (Chess Hard held-out: Fable 5 37.5 to 73.3, Opus 5 25.0 to 66.4) and out-of-distribution gains are consistently smaller than in-distribution ones (Go Fable 5 20 to 80 ID against 0 to 50 OOD; Hex Sol 40 to 77.5 ID against 28.1 to 78.1 OOD). But two same-protocol recipients declined: GPT-5.6 Luna on NetHack fell about 210 to 120 and GPT-5.6 Sol about 570 to 420, where Sol is the most plastic model on board games. Artefact reuse also dissociated from success: Luna took ~98% of relevant chess decisions without using artefacts, versus 2-6% for the models that actually improved.

nodes.title: Loom's own paired lesson A/B: 53 null, 4 'wins' that are control-arm crashes, 3 genuine losses, 0 genuine wins
nodes.body: The loop already runs the experiment rsi-019 asks for and the result is legible per event. 60 lesson.impact events pair a treated attempt (saw lessons) against an unexposed control of the same round; resolving both arms by attempt id gives 53 pairs where both arms passed (delta 0), 4 with delta +1 where the control arm errored ('child session ended in error with no diagnostic' or 'dispatcher disposed'), and 3 with delta -1 where the treated arm genuinely failed (loom-self2 round 7, all three quarantined for 'paired evidence: gain -1 over 5 use(s), 1 harm(s)'). nodes.title: Loom's pass rate falls 62.2% to 25% by round, but 27.9% of attempts are infra errors
nodes.body: Computed per round index over all 452 attempts: round 1 62.2% (n=135), round 2 58.9% (n=107), round 3 36.5% (n=52), round 4 33.3% (n=24), rounds 5-10 40.0, 40.0, 37.5, 25.0, 33.3, 40.0, round 11 20.0%, round 13 25.0% (n=8). It would be easy to read as decay, and it is not: later rounds are a different task mix (median 3 evalset tasks per campaign, 2.48 mean), and 126 of 452 attempts (27.9%) carry an error string - 80 'child session ended in error with no diagnostic', 21 timeouts at 600000ms, 14 'dispatcher disposed', 6 'cannot get property sessions'. With 28% of rows scoring zero for transport reasons, any longitudinal curve from this log is an availability curve. The honest statement is that the log cannot separate decay from attrition, which is exactly the gap an external decay study would fill.
